title: Potassium iodide (KI) in a radiation emergency: who, when, how much, and what it does not do
asks: should I take potassium iodide after a nuclear accident
when do I take iodine pills
are iodine tablets an anti radiation pill
KI pills fallout do they help
can pregnant women or babies take potassium iodide
how long does a KI dose last
who should not take iodine tablets
nuke plant accident take KI now or wait
how much potassium iodide should I take
KI dose for a child or a baby
answer: KI protects only the thyroid gland, and only from radioactive iodine. It has no impact on the body's uptake of other radioactive materials and gives no protection against external radiation of any kind.
Use KI only as an addition to evacuation, sheltering and control of food, not in place of them.
When: KI works best when taken before, or just as, the radioactive cloud passes. It may still have a substantial protective effect even if taken 3 or 4 hours after exposure.
The protective effect lasts approximately 24 hours. For best protection KI is dosed daily until there is no longer a risk of significant exposure to radioactive iodine by breathing or eating.
How much to take, by age (FDA): adults 130 mg. Children over 3 through 12 years: 65 mg. Children over 1 month through 3 years: 32 mg. Babies from birth through 1 month: 16 mg.
Teenagers: FDA's standard dose for all school-age children is 65 mg, but adolescents approaching adult size (over 70 kg) should take the full adult dose, 130 mg.

KI tablets come in two strengths, 65 mg and 130 mg. For a smaller dose, a tablet can be dissolved in liquid and the right amount of the liquid given. FDA's example: if a 130 mg tablet is dissolved in 8 ounces of liquid, one ounce contains about 16 mg of KI. For babies, KI may be diluted in milk, formula or water.

If exact doses are not practical: FDA says absolute precision in dosing is generally not critical to safety or effectiveness, and that higher doses (up to 130 mg) are equally effective and, particularly among school-age children, extremely safe. But pay attention to the dose for infants and keep to FDA's doses for them where feasible: too much iodine can cause temporary hypothyroidism (an underactive thyroid).

Who needs it most: fetuses, infants and young children are at the greatest risk and may be harmed by small amounts of radioactive iodine. Pregnant women should be given KI for their own protection and for that of the fetus.
Adults over 40 need take KI only if a very large radiation dose to the thyroid is projected.

Repeat doses should be avoided for newborns (first month of life) and pregnant women, and for breastfeeding mothers except during continuing severe contamination. These groups should get priority for the other protections: sheltering, evacuation and control of the food supply.
Once the cloud has passed, protection from radioactive iodine in food is best achieved by food control, not by repeated doses of KI.
warnings: KI is not a general protection against radiation.
People with a known iodine sensitivity should avoid KI, as should people with dermatitis herpetiformis or hypocomplementemic vasculitis.

As a rule, people with a known allergy to KI or with existing thyroid disease (for example Graves' disease, thyroid nodules, Hashimoto's thyroiditis) should avoid KI. Most are adults, who have little or no risk of thyroid cancer from the exposure and may incur substantial risks from taking KI.

quotes.text: KI provides protection only for the thyroid from radioiodines. It has no impact on the uptake by the body of other radioactive materials and provides no protection against external irradiation of any kind. FDA emphasizes that the use of KI should be as an adjunct to evacuation (itself not always feasible), sheltering, and control of foodstuffs.

KI is recommended for use as an adjunct to other emergency measures, such as evacuation and control of the food supply to avoid ingestion of contaminated foodstuffs. When used correctly, KI can prevent or reduce the uptake of radioiodine by the thyroid gland. KI provides optimal protection when administered immediately prior to or in conjunction with passage of a radioactive cloud.

For optimal protection against inhaled radioiodines, KI should be administered before or immediately coincident with passage of the radioactive cloud, though KI may still have a substantial protective effect even if taken 3 or 4 hours after exposure.

The protective effect of KI lasts approximately 24 hours. For optimal prophylaxis, KI should therefore be dosed daily, until a risk of significant exposure to radioiodines by either inhalation or ingestion no longer exists. Individuals intolerant of KI at protective doses, and neonates, pregnant and lactating women (in whom repeat administration of KI raises particular safety issues, see below) should be given priority with regard to other protective measures (i.e., sheltering, evacuation, and control of the food supply).

FDA guidance recommends graded dosing by age, with neonates receiving the lowest dose (16 mg daily) and adults receiving the highest (130 mg). FDA approved KI tablets are available in two dosage strengths: 65 and 130 mg. At a minimum, dosing based on FDA guidance would require either splitting tablets or dissolving tablets in liquids.
Threshold Thyroid Radioactive Exposures and Recommended Doses of KI for Different Risk Groups

Children over 3 through 12 yrs 65 1/2 1 Over 1 month through 3 years 32 1/4 1/2 Birth through 1 month 16 1/8 1/4 *Adolescents approaching adult size (> 70 kg) should receive the full adult dose (130 mg).

The downward KI dose adjustment by age group, based on body size considerations, adheres to the principle of minimum effective dose. The recommended standard dose of KI for all schoolage children is the same (65 mg). However, adolescents approaching adult size (i.e., >70 kg) should receive the full adult dose (130 mg) for maximal block of thyroid radioiodine uptake. Neonates ideally should receive the lowest dose (16 mg) of KI.

If a graded dosing approach is considered, how does FDA suggest that fractional doses (i.e., 65, 32, 16 mg) be administered? A3: KI tablets can be dissolved in liquids and the appropriate volume administered. For example, if a 130 mg tablet were dissolved in 8 ounces of liquid, one ounce would contain about 16 mg of KI. FDA has conducted studies of the palatability, solubility, and stability of KI dissolved in a number of different liquids, including juice and formula.
KI from tablets (either whole or fractions) or as fresh saturated KI solution may be diluted in milk, formula, or water and the appropriate volume administered to babies.
Emergency planners and others should understand that absolute precision in dosing is generally not critical to safety or efficacy (see also question 4).
FDA has made recommendations on the lowest effective dose. Higher doses (e.g., up to 130 mg) would be equally effective and, particularly among school-age children, extremely safe
However, we continue to emphasize attention to KI dosing in infants. Excess iodine intake can lead to transient iodine-induced hypothyroidism.

In summary, if local emergency planners conclude that graded dosing is logistically impractical, FDA believes that for populations at risk for radioiodine exposure, the overall benefits of taking up to 130 mg of KI instead of the lower doses recommended for certain age groups far exceed the small risks of overdosing. However, where feasible, adherence to FDA guidance should be attempted when dosing infants.
The data suggest that the risk of thyroid cancer is inversely related to age. Fetuses, infants, and young children are at greatest risk and may be harmed by small amounts of radioiodine.

Pregnant women should be given KI for their own protection and for that of the fetus, as iodine (whether stable or radioactive) readily crosses the placenta. However, because of the risk of blocking fetal thyroid function with excess stable iodine, repeat dosing with KI of pregnant women should be avoided.
Repeat dosing of KI should be avoided in the neonate to minimize the risk of hypothyroidism during that critical phase of brain development

Therefore, repeat dosing with KI should be avoided in the lactating mother, except during continuing severe contamination. If repeat dosing of the mother is necessary, the nursing neonate should be monitored as recommended above.

Although special precautions should be taken when administering KI to pregnant women and newborns within the first month of life (adherence to the recommended dose, avoidance of repeat dosing, and monitoring of thyroid function in neonates), the benefits of short-term administration of KI as a thyroid blocking agent far exceed the risks of administration to any age group.
Note that adults over 40 need take KI only in the case of a projected large internal radiation dose to the thyroid (>500 cGy) to prevent hypothyroidism.

Thyroid irradiation in older adults (e.g., over 40 years of age) is associated with an extremely low incidence of cancer. Therefore, KI is only recommended if a very large internal radioactive dose to the thyroid is projected.

Prevention of thyroid uptake of ingested radioiodines, once the plume has passed and radiation protection measures (including KI) are in place, is best accomplished by food control measures and not by repeated administration of KI.

In addition, persons with known iodine sensitivity should avoid KI, as should individuals with dermatitis herpetiformis and hypocomplementemic vasculitis, extremely rare conditions associated with an increased risk of iodine hypersensitivity.

As a rule, however, individuals with known allergy to KI or with pre-existing thyroid disease (e.g., Graves' disease, thyroid nodules, Hashimoto's thyroiditis) that might predispose them to adverse reactions should avoid KI. Most likely these will be adults, who have little or no risk of developing thyroid cancer from radioactive exposure to the thyroid and who may, in these cases, incur substantial risks from taking KI.

conflict: TIMING: FDA Guidance 2001 says best before or as the cloud passes, may still have a substantial protective effect even if taken 3 or 4 hours after exposure, and that even delayed doses may help if the release is protracted; ATP 4-02.11 (2026) para 19-96 says KI 'is only effective if taken within four hours before or after exposure'; ATP 4-02.83 (2014) and AFRRI 2022 say before or within 4 hours of exposure. THYROID DISEASE: FDA Q&A 2002 says such individuals 'should avoid KI'; FDA Guidance 2001 says they 'should be treated with caution, especially if dosing extends beyond a few days', and ATP 4-02.83 says use with caution and careful medical monitoring. REPEAT DOSES AND DURATION: FDA 2001 says dose daily while the risk continues, but avoid repeat doses in newborns, pregnant and breastfeeding women; ATP 4-02.83 says a one-time dose is usually all that is needed; HHS Ship's Medicine Chest 2003 says 'One (1) 130 mg tablet once a day. Take for 10 days unless directed otherwise by State or local public health authorities.' FEMA P-2064 (2020) and the two FEMA nuclear detonation guides do not mention potassium iodide. DOSES (added in revision; the card shows FDA's doses): FDA Guidance 2001 and FDA Q&A 2002 grade the dose by age: adults 130 mg, school-age children 65 mg (adolescents approaching adult size, over 70 kg, 130 mg), over 1 month through 3 years 32 mg, birth through 1 month 16 mg. HOW THE DOSES ARE QUOTED: the adult, school-age, adult-size adolescent and newborn doses are quoted from FDA prose (Q&A question 4; Guidance section IV.B). The exact age bands come from three rows of the FDA Guidance table ('Children over 3 through 12 yrs 65', 'Over 1 month through 3 years 32', 'Birth through 1 month 16'), which extract in order: age group, KI dose in mg, then the number of 130 mg and of 65 mg tablets. The 32 mg dose for over 1 month through 3 years rests on that table row alone (Q&A question 3 names the fractional doses as 65, 32 and 16 mg). The upper rows of the same table (adults over 40, adults over 18 through 40, pregnant or lactating women, adolescents over 12 through 18) extract with their dose cells out of order, so the card does not quote them: it gives no separate line for pregnant or breastfeeding women (the table lists them at the adult dose) and takes the adolescent dose from the prose and the table footnote. The same three rows also give tablet fractions (65 mg is 1/2 of a 130 mg tablet or 1 of a 65 mg tablet; 32 mg is 1/4 or 1/2; 16 mg is 1/8 or 1/4; column order confirmed by reading the page with pdftotext -table), but the column headings extract out of order in the text the build checks, so the card does not show the fractions and gives FDA's dissolving example instead. The owner may want them added. ATP 4-02.83 (2014) Table 4-5 lists the same doses (adults and pregnant or lactating women 130 mg per day, children and adolescents 3 to 18 years 65 mg, infants 1 month to 3 years 32 mg, neonates 16 mg) without the note on adult-size adolescents; its text is split between labels and doses, so it is not quoted. Owner to confirm the age lines against the FDA table itself (printed page 6 of the Guidance). OTHER DOSE STATEMENTS IN THE KIT: HHS Ship's Medicine Chest 2003 gives only 'One (1) 130 mg tablet once a day' (a book for adult crew); ATP 4-02.83's drug table gives the adult dose and says to consult FDA recommended doses for infants and children; ORNL-5037 Nuclear War Survival Skills (1979) gives the older scheme of approximately 130 mg for adults and children and 65 mg for infants less than 12 months old, which FDA Guidance 2001 says it revised (its 1982 amounts were '130 mg per day for adults and children above 1 year of age and 65 mg per day for children below 1 year of age'); FDA Guidance 2001 notes that WHO's 1999 guidelines give 130 mg to adolescents over 12 years. AFRRI 2022 has a KI dose table that is an image with no text. FDA Q&A 2002 says that higher doses (up to 130 mg) are equally effective and that precision is 'generally not critical', while asking for attention to dosing in infants; the card shows both statements.

review.notes: Re-review 2026-11-25 (claude-opus-5-5 xhigh). Previous finding fixed: A5 to A8 give the dose by age, how to make the small doses and what to do if exact doses are impractical, attributed to FDA. Dose extraction judged trustworthy. I checked the text cache and pdftotext -layout of FDA Guidance 2001 printed p.6: the three quoted rows sit under the 'KI dose (mg)' column (65, 32, 16), followed by the counts of 130 mg and 65 mg tablets (1/2 and 1, 1/4 and 1/2, 1/8 and 1/4), and each row is arithmetically consistent (65 = half a 130 = one 65; 32 = a quarter of 130 = half a 65; 16 = an eighth of 130 = a quarter of 65). The same doses come out cleanly, in row order, in ATP 4-02.83 Table 4-5 (130, 130, 130, 65, 32, 16 mg per day for adults over 40, adults 18 to 40, pregnant or lactating women, ages 3 to 18, 1 month to 3 years, birth to 1 month), and FDA prose independently gives 130 mg adults, 65 mg school-age, 130 mg for adolescents over 70 kg, 16 mg neonates and names 65, 32 and 16 mg as the fractional doses. The upper FDA rows are scrambled and the card rightly does not quote them. All other lines checked in context against FDA Guidance 2001 and Q&A 2002. Recommended, not blocking: (1) W3 shows FDA Q&A 2002's 'as a rule ... should avoid KI' for thyroid disease without attribution, while FDA Guidance 2001 and ATP 4-02.83 (2014) say use it with caution and careful medical monitoring, especially beyond a few days. It is listed in conflict and is the conservative choice for adults, but attribute it (FDA, 2002) and consider showing the caution alternative; W3 also drops FDA's qualifier 'that might predispose them to adverse reactions'. (2) Pregnant or breastfeeding women have no dose line: 'adults 130 mg' covers most, but both tables put them at 130 mg whatever their age, while a pregnant teenager would read 65 mg from the teen line; ATP 4-02.83 Table 4-5 is clean enough to quote if the owner wants that line. (3) ATP 4-02.83 adds 'A seafood or shellfish allergy does not necessarily indicate allergy to iodine', which would prevent needless avoidance under W2. Kind fact correct; all asks answered; no PDF junk. previous review: (verdict fail, by claude-opus-5-5 (xhigh), independent review 2026-11-24) Problem (point c): no dose. The card answers 'should I take potassium iodide', 'when do I take iodine pills' and 'can pregnant women or babies take' but never says how much, and the right amount depends on age (too much in newborns risks hypothyroidism, which the card itself raises in A7). The conflict field says the FDA dose table extracts as scrambled cells, but clean text exists: FDA Q&A 2002 Q4 'graded dosing by age, with neonates receiving the lowest dose (16 mg daily) and adults receiving the highest (130 mg)', Q3 lists the fractional doses '65, 32, 16 mg' and A3 gives the dissolve-in-liquid method; ATP 4-02.83 gives a daily table. Fix: add the age doses (or at minimum 'adults 130 mg once a day, newborns 16 mg; children in between by age; follow the package') with those quotes, or a hard pointer to a KI dose card. Confirmed in context: FDA Guidance 2001 and Q&A 2002 (thyroid only, adjunct to evacuation, sheltering and food control; timing incl. 3-4 h; 24 h effect, daily dosing; age risk; pregnancy; over-40 threshold; repeat-dose limits for newborns, pregnant and lactating women; food control after the plume; who should avoid). Timing, thyroid-disease and repeat-dose disagreements (ATP 4-02.11 four-hour window, ATP 4-02.83 one dose, HHS 10 days) are listed. No PDF junk. kind 'fact' is right.
